Image shows T1-T3 NMR images of a rat hind limb. The muscle compartments of the rat hind limb were delineated by MRI (Figures 4a and 4b). Note that these images were acquired while the rat was in a resting state. The muscles that were identified were as follows: T3 (clover), tibia, and femur. Muscle tissue has varying T1 values depending on muscle fiber organization. In particular, muscles with a high density of tendons fibers have a higher T1 value (darker signals), while muscles with a higher density of fascicles have a lower T1 signal (light signals.) Signal intensity differences reflected muscle fiber organization. The brightness/contrast of muscle compartments could reflect fiber organization.

Illustration of the method used for evaluating the contrast enhancement rate (C-E ratio): The darker areas surrounding the spinal cord and nerve roots represent the paravertebral muscles and spinal cord–paraspinal fascia (CSA) [52]. The darker areas surrounding the vertebral body represent the vertebral bone marrow. The darker areas around the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the CSF space represent the CSF and CSF space (CSA). C-E ratio = contrast enhancement rate = (CSA surrounding spinal cord)–(darkest area surrounding spinal cord) / (darkest area surrounding spinal cord + CSA surrounding spinal cord). Measurement sites and methods were as follows: Measurement 1: Horizontal base width (H-B): Distance between the most anterior point of nasal base and most posterior point of nasal base. Measurement 2: Horizontal nasal width (H-N): Distance between the most anterior point of nasal base and most anterior point of nasal septum. Measurement 3: Vertical nasal height (V-N): Distance between most anterior nasal septum to most posterior point of nasal septum. Measurement 4: Nasal septum angle (NSA): Angle formed by intersection point between midsagital plane plane and nasal septum. Measurement 5: Nasal floor width (N-F): Horizontal distance between most anterior point of nasal floor and most posterior point of nasal floor.

Abdominal CT scan reveals a small bowel obstruction secondary to intussusception. Intussusception is a rare complication following laparoscopic gastric banding and can result in bowel ischemia. Intussusception is defined as the invagination of one bowel segment into another. It may be caused by adhesions, tumors, inflammatory bowel disease, volvulus or intraluminal mass. Intraluminal masses may be bezoars, fecalomas or other ingested substances. Surgical intervention to remove intraluminal mass can release intussusception. Intussusception may also be caused by inflammatory bowel disease. There are different forms of inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis

This figure illustrates the measurement techniques for assessing laryngeal motion during VFSS. Using fluoroscopy, the VFSS is placed over the larynx (indicated by the 'VFSS' in red). Using a coordinate system, we recorded the distances between key landmarks on VFSS, including C2-4 length, the distance between key landmarks on the larynx, and the positioning of key landmarks on the larynx. In addition, we recorded distances (vertical and horizontal) between key landmarks on VFSS and key landmarks on larynx. Using an attached sensor, we recorded vertical and horizontal displacement of VFSS over time. These parameters were recorded simultaneously for each VFSS test. Abbreviations: VFSS: videofluoroscopic swallow test; SEMG: subcutaneous electromyography; C2-4: cervical vertebrae 2-4; Y coordinate: vertical movement; X- coordinate: horizontal movement.
